summary.summary: This is the investment-side appendix of Shropshire's treasury outturn report, covering only cash investment strategy and performance for 2025/26, not the council's debt or borrowing position. Bank Rate fell in three 0.25% steps during the year (May, August, December) from 4.50% to 3.75%, and the council's internal treasury team achieved an average return of 4.05% against a SONIA overnight benchmark of 4.19% -- a shortfall of 0.14%, attributed to holding very short-term cash balances for liquidity. At 31 March 2026 the whole £54.2m cash portfolio matured within one month, with nothing held in any longer maturity band. No debt, CFR, borrowing or capital figures appear in this appendix; those would sit in the companion treasury outturn sections not included in this cached document.

compliance.notes: Strong on the technical prudential/treasury indicators and the liability benchmark - a fully-charted 10-year benchmark (LB-01/02 = 3), thorough capex/CFR reconciliation (PI-01/02 = 3), a robust CDS-overlay creditworthiness policy (INV-03 = 3) and a detailed, full-council-approved MRP policy (MRP-02 = 3). Governance and reporting are solid (three-stage Audit&Governance/Cabinet/Council approval, quarterly monitoring, 2021 Codes formally adopted for 2026/27). Weakest areas: (1) the financing-costs-to-net-revenue-stream ratio (PI-07, a CORE affordability indicator) is entirely absent - striking given Shropshire declared a financial emergency on 10 Sep 2025 and its CFR nearly doubles (591m->1,080m) on assumed Exceptional Financial Support; (2) knowledge & skills (KS-01, core) is only a training reference, not a formal policy/schedule; (3) the commercial/non-treasury core items (COM-01 no-borrow-for-yield statement, COM-03 quantified proportionality) are only referenced, and several commercial disclosures (COM-02/07/09) are absent from the documents read - partly because the packet's 'capital strategy' is a 2025/26 in-year review stock-take rather than the full Capital Strategy 2026/27, so the detailed commercial/proportionality disclosures that normally live there could not be evidenced. Also missing: borrowing-in-advance-of-need policy (BOR-02), sterling-borrowing statement (BOR-03), audit-qualification flag (RPT-05) and a derivatives policy (RISK-06).

gaps.evidence: TMSS p.4: financing costs named as an indicator to be split GF/HRA, but no ratio-of-financing-costs-to-net-revenue-stream table or figures anywhere in the TMSS

TMSS p.3-4: commercial initiatives/loans to third parties classed as non-treasury and separated from treasury; low risk appetite (p.2); capstrat requires council-funded capital to 'improve the Council's financial position or be operationally essential'

TMSS p.16 (S151 role): 'ensuring the proportionality of all investments so that the authority does not undertake a level of investing which exposes the authority to an excessive level of risk compared to its financial resources'

news_drafts.headline: Shropshire lists £121m of 2026-27 transformation spending to be funded by borrowing under exceptional support
news_drafts.lead:
Shropshire Council's transformation programme is listed at £121m of expenditure for 2026-27, to be funded through borrowing under an approval for exceptional financial support (EFS), which is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The figure is in Appendix C, on prudential borrowing approvals, in the papers for the Cabinet meeting on 2 December 2026.

The table shows the programme in three successive years: £26.82m for 2024-25 and £61.86m for 2025-26, both also funded through borrowing under EFS approval. The 2026-27 line is the largest of the three. It has a 20-year life, and the table shows minimum revenue provision, the amount a council must set aside from each year's budget to pay off past borrowing, first charged in 2025/26.

The council's treasury strategy mid-year review for 2026/27 lists "Impact of financing Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)" among its key treasury risks, with a mitigation column alongside. The text provided does not give the size or timing of the support.

news_drafts.headline: Shropshire says £121m of exceptional financial support let it set a balanced 2026/27 budget
news_drafts.lead:
Shropshire Council's chief finance officer says the council could not have set a balanced budget for 2026/27 without exceptional financial support, the government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The statement is in the draft medium term financial plan for 2027-2032, before the Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 30 November.

The plan says: "Ultimately, without this EFS, the Council would have been unable to set a balanced budget for the year and it would have been necessary for the s151 Officer to issue a s114 notice." Here EFS is exceptional financial support, s151 Officer is the chief finance officer, and a s114 notice is a section 114 notice. The government has approved £121m of support in principle for 2026/27. The council received £71m for 2025/26.

According to the paper, the support filled structural deficits in adults' and children's social care and removed unachievable savings targets from the base budget. It also allowed the council to rebuild its capacity. The chief finance officer expects a financial sustainability strategy to take at least five years to deliver, with the aim of reducing the council's reliance on the support.

news_drafts.headline: Shropshire's 2026-27 exceptional financial support estimate falls to £87m from £121m approved
news_drafts.lead:
Shropshire Council estimated by July 2026 that it would need £87m of exceptional financial support in 2026-27, against the £121m approved by government. The support is permission from government to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. For 2025-26 the estimate had fallen to £61m, against £71m approved. The council's annual assurance report says the 2026-27 figure came down after its interim section 151 officer reviewed the assumptions in the medium-term financial plan.

The 2026-27 budget was underpinned by a council tax increase of 8.99% and £121m of support, both approved by government. The projected requirement is £99m for 2027-28 and £121m for 2028-29.

The Audit and Governance Committee also has its external auditor's findings on the 2025-26 accounts. The auditor found no significant issues and reported that expenditure was in accordance with a draft letter from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The council is still awaiting the final capitalisation direction, which is government permission to treat day-to-day spending as capital spending so that borrowing or asset sales can pay for it. The auditor says it needs that letter before issuing its audit opinion, and expects to report on 30 January 2027.

findings.headline: The open risk on having adequate resource for additional dashboard work is rated Medium.
findings.detail: The risk register lists resourcing for the extra dashboard workload as a Medium-rated open risk, alongside an issue on how to resource dashboard queries so the team is not overwhelmed and timescales are met. A new Communications and Governance Team Leader started in August 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Pensions Dashboard Monthly Report for Committee - Aug to Oct 2026
findings.headline: The dashboard policy is shown as December 2026 'On Track' in the milestone table, while the narrative gives early 2027 for finalisation.
findings.detail: The milestone table shows the Dashboard Policy target as December 2026 with status On Track. The narrative says the work is on hold because other policies have taken priority, that it is being progressed with South Yorkshire Pension Fund, and that it will be finalised in early 2027.
findings.matters: A policy deadline stated in one place as December 2026 and in another as early 2027 is the kind of timing difference a finance director would want clarified before relying on the schedule.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Pensions Dashboard Monthly Report for Committee - Aug to Oct 2026
findings.headline: AVC single-source dashboard implementation dates slipped, and the AVC solution is in Altair Test but not yet deployed to Live.
findings.detail: The report attributes the slippage to issues with the Heywood Altair interface. It says the AVC solution is now in place in Altair Test, with issues being investigated by Heywood, so it is not yet deployed to Live. The AVC error messages from the dashboard are recorded as a problem Heywood has raised.
findings.matters: Supplier-side interface delays on a shared administration platform are the kind of dependency other funds on the same system would need to plan around for their own dashboard go-live dates.

findings.headline: Shropshire's connection to the pensions dashboard is established and data is being sent to it.
findings.detail: The report lists the connection as established and data as successfully being sent to the dashboard in this period. It also records that the ISP connection deadline was not met but is now closed in the risk register.

findings.paper_title: Shropshire County Pension Fund - 2026 Climate Related Disclosures
findings.headline: Corporate fixed income normalised financed emissions rose from 37.9 to 67.5 tCO2e per £m invested, which the paper says partly reflects a change of investment strategy rather than a like-for-like deterioration.
findings.detail: The Fund moved from its previous Sterling and Global investment-grade strategy to the Global Active Investment Grade Corporate Bond Multi Manager Fund, which has a different universe and a materially higher-carbon benchmark. The paper says the old strategy reported 37.2 against 67.2 for the new fund on a like-for-like basis.
findings.matters: A change in investment manager or strategy can move emissions headlines independently of underlying company emissions, so peers reading a fixed-income climate metric need to check whether the strategy itself changed.
findings.figures: 37.9 to 67.5 tCO2e per £m invested (combined basis); 37.2 (previous strategy); 67.2 (current fund); WACI 139.9 to 210.7 tCO2e per $m sales
findings.quote: On a combined basis, normalised financed emissions increased from 37.9 to 67.5
